title: Capital Allocation: How Much in One Deal, How Much in One Kind of Deal, How Much Borrowed
summary: Capital allocation is three decisions: how large each position is, how much of your wealth sits in one kind of risk, and how much personal borrowing sits behind it all. A developer can be right about every project and still be ruined by getting those three wrong. This lesson gives the concepts and a way to set limits before the next deal arrives.
body:
The question is never only whether a deal is good. It is how much of you should be in it. A good deal sized too large can end a career that a mediocre deal sized correctly would not even dent.

Recall

Q. What are the three liquidity tiers?

A. Tier 1, cash available within days for living costs; tier 2, assets that become cash within months at modest cost, sized to contingent calls such as guarantees; tier 3, long-term illiquid capital such as project equity and land.

Q. Name the six links in the project risk chain.

A. Allocation, transfer, retention, resolution, proof and challenge: the contract allocates, insurance and bonds fund, the register owns the rest, the dispute ladder settles, records prove and independent review tests.

Q. What is consequential loss, and why do contracts exclude it?

A. Indirect loss flowing from a breach, such as lost profit or rent. Contracts exclude it because it can be large and hard to foresee, and parties want a known ceiling. What counts as consequential depends on the wording and the governing law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Warrick, with Roman joining for the lender's view. Last week built the shape of your wealth: layers, tiers and currencies. This week decides how much goes where. Developers are unusually exposed, because deals are lumpy, each one is large relative to the developer's net worth, and the developer usually guarantees part of the debt. Three numbers decide survival: position size, concentration and personal leverage. Everything here is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Position sizing: how much in one deal

In plain English: decide in advance the most you can lose on any single deal without it changing your life.

Professionally, position sizing sets the share of your wealth committed to one investment, including the equity you put in and the realistic call on any guarantee you sign. The disciplined version starts from loss, not from opportunity: first decide the most you are willing to lose on one position, then work out how large the position can be given how badly it could go. A practitioner habit is to cap the realistic worst-case loss on any one deal at a fixed share of net worth; the share is a personal choice, not a standard.

Worked example, hypothetical round numbers. Net worth is 5,000,000 dollars, and the developer decides no single deal may cost more than 15 percent of it in a severe case: 750,000 dollars. A new project asks for 1,000,000 dollars of equity plus a cost-overrun guarantee with a realistic severe call of 500,000. Severe loss: the equity could be wiped out in a deep downturn, and the guarantee called, so 1,500,000 dollars, or 30 percent of net worth. That is twice the limit. The developer can take half the equity, 500,000, and negotiate the guarantee down to a 250,000 severe case: 750,000 in total, inside the limit. The same deal, half the size, no longer threatens the household.

Say that out loud now.

Concentration: how much in one kind of risk

In plain English: five deals that all fail for the same reason are one deal, not five.

Concentration is the share of your wealth exposed to one common risk, such as one city, one asset type, one lender, one partner, one currency or one point in the cycle. Diversification, spreading across risks that do not move together, reduces concentration. For a developer, perfect diversification is neither possible nor desirable, because expertise is local and focused. The goal is not to remove concentration but to know it, name it and cap it.

Second worked example, hypothetical. A developer holds equity in four projects worth 1,000,000 dollars each, all condominiums in one city, all funded by the same lender, all selling to buyers who depend on the same local employers. On paper, four positions. In a local downturn, the pre-sales fall together, the lender tightens on all four at once, and the guarantees are called together. The concentration is effectively 100 percent in one risk. A developer with the same four projects across two cities and two asset types, a rental building and a condominium, still has concentration, but a shock to one city or one product hits half the portfolio rather than all of it.

Personal leverage: how much is borrowed behind you

In plain English: borrowing at the project level is normal; borrowing against yourself to fund equity multiplies every loss.

Personal leverage is debt that you personally owe or guarantee, including loans taken to fund your equity contributions, margin on investments, and guarantees of project loans. Project debt without recourse to you is the project's risk; personal leverage is yours. Layering them is where developers get hurt: a personal loan funds the equity in a project that is itself highly levered, and a fall in the project's value hits the equity first, which then cannot repay the personal loan. Roman's lens: count the layers of borrowing between your house and the building. Each one magnifies the movement of the one below it.

Putting the three together

The three decisions interact. A small position in a concentrated, levered portfolio can still be dangerous, because the other positions fail with it and the borrowing reaches you. A large position can be survivable if it is unlevered and the rest of your wealth sits in different risks. So the limits are set together: the severe-case loss per deal, the share of wealth in any one common risk, and the total personal borrowing and guarantees, checked against the tiers you sized last week. Applied to the earlier example, the developer taking half the equity also checks that the new project is not in the same city, with the same lender, as his existing two; if it is, the three projects are one exposure, and the 15 percent limit applies to the group, not to each project.

How the best do it

Disciplined long-term investors and well-run family offices typically write their limits in an investment policy statement before they see a deal: maximum position size, maximum exposure to one market or sponsor, and maximum leverage. They then measure every new opportunity against the policy, rather than writing the policy around the opportunity. A small developer can copy that with a one-page allocation policy: three numbers, written in calm conditions, and a rule that changing a limit requires a cooling-off period and a second opinion.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the way you fund a position, debt or equity, personally or through a company, changes the tax treatment of interest and returns; get advice before you borrow to invest. Liability: personal leverage and guarantees are where project failures become personal failures. Banking: lenders assess your concentration and other guarantees, and a disciplined allocation improves your terms. Governance: put the allocation limits in writing and require a deliberate process to breach them. Estate: concentrated, levered positions are hard for heirs or executors to manage or sell. Exit: a smaller position in a deal gives you more choice about when to exit, because you are never forced.

Professional sign-off required: licensed financial adviser, on allocation limits; lawyer, on the guarantee terms behind each position.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing a position by how good the deal looks instead of by how badly it could go. The control is to set the maximum severe-case loss per deal, as a share of net worth, before you see the next deal.

The beginner's mistake

Counting four projects as diversification when they share the same city, lender and buyers. Group positions by what would make them fail together.

Callback

In Week 37, Priya taught the capital stack and how losses climb it from the bottom. Personal leverage puts another layer beneath your equity in that stack. The losses that climb the stack reach your equity first, and personal leverage carries them from there into your house.

Recap

Capital allocation is three decisions: position size, set from the severe-case loss you can bear; concentration, grouped by common risk; and personal leverage, counted layer by layer. Write the three limits down before the next deal.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Long-Term Capital Management in 1998, brilliant people and too much borrowing.
checklist: I have a written maximum severe-case loss per deal, as a share of net worth.
I count both equity and realistic guarantee calls in each position.
I group my positions by what would make them fail together.
I know my exposure to each city, asset type, lender and partner.
I count every layer of borrowing between my house and each building.
My allocation limits are in a one-page policy written in calm conditions.
Changing a limit requires a cooling-off period and a second opinion.
I will review my limits with a licensed adviser before acting.
head: Field checklist
speak: Capital allocation is three decisions. Position size: how much of my wealth is in one deal, counting the equity and the realistic guarantee call. I set it from loss, not opportunity: first decide the most I can lose on one deal, say 15 percent of a hypothetical 5,000,000 net worth, then size the position so the severe case stays inside it. Concentration: five deals that fail for the same reason are one deal, so I group positions by common risk, city, asset type, lender, partner, currency and cycle, and cap each group. Personal leverage: debt I owe or guarantee, especially loans that fund my equity in projects that are already levered, which multiplies every loss. I write the three limits on one page before I see the next deal, and changing a limit takes a cooling-off period and a second opinion.
terms: Position sizing — setting how much of your wealth goes into one investment, starting from the loss you can bear.
Concentration — the share of your wealth exposed to one common risk that could make several positions fail together.
Personal leverage — debt you owe or guarantee personally, including borrowing to fund your own equity.

hostile.q: It's a great deal. Why are you only taking half the equity?
hostile.a: Because sized at the full 1,000,000 dollars of equity plus the guarantee, the severe case would cost me 30 percent of my net worth, twice my written limit. At half the equity and a reduced guarantee, the severe case is inside the limit. If the deal is as good as we both think, I still do well; if it goes badly, I am still here for the next one.

title: Long-Term Capital Management, 1998: Brilliant Models, Too Much Borrowing
summary: Long-Term Capital Management, a hedge fund founded in 1994 with partners who included two future Nobel laureates in economics, lost most of its capital in 1998 after Russia's default triggered a flight from risk. Its trades were not foolish one by one; together, at its leverage, they could not survive a market that moved against all of them at once. In September 1998 its lenders recapitalised it in a rescue organised by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
body:
Long-Term Capital Management was run by some of the most sophisticated people in finance. It failed not because its people were careless but because it borrowed so much against positions that, in a crisis, all moved the same way at the same time.

Recall

Q. What is the difference between position size and concentration?

A. Position size is how much is in one investment. Concentration is how much of your wealth is exposed to one common risk across many investments.

Q. What does Rule 85 say?

A. Never fund a long-term asset with short-term debt in a currency other than the one it earns, and never keep the emergency reserve only in a currency or banking system the feared shock could devalue or freeze.

Q. What is a liquidated damages clause?

A. A clause that fixes in advance the sum payable for a defined breach, usually delay, often as a daily rate with a cap, as a genuine estimate of loss rather than a penalty.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Ford, with Roman for the finance view. You are not running a hedge fund, and this is not a lesson about trading. It is the clearest real case of what leverage and hidden concentration do to intelligent people. The same mechanics can destroy a developer who borrows personally to fund equity in several projects that share one risk. The facts below are the widely reported ones; detailed accounts of the episode are available for anyone who wants the full story.

Step 1: Timeline

Long-Term Capital Management, known as LTCM, was founded in 1994 by a well-known bond trader and a team that included Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the Nobel prize in economics in 1997. It made large, carefully modelled bets that small price differences between related securities would narrow over time. Its early returns were very strong. In August 1998 Russia defaulted on some of its debt and devalued its currency, investors worldwide fled to the safest assets, and the price differences LTCM had bet would narrow instead widened sharply. Over the following weeks the fund lost most of its capital. In September 1998 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York convened a group of banks and brokers, who together put in fresh capital, about 3.6 billion dollars, in return for most of the fund, to allow an orderly wind-down.

Step 2: Key decisions

Two decisions mattered most. First, to use very high leverage: each trade earned a small margin, so the fund borrowed many times its own capital to make the returns large. Second, to keep adding similar trades, in many markets, that all depended on the same underlying condition: calm markets in which investors were willing to hold riskier assets. The trades looked diversified across countries and instruments. They shared one risk.

Step 3: Assumptions

The models assumed that the relationships between prices observed in the past would broadly hold, that extreme moves were rare, and that the fund could always borrow and could always sell. Each assumption held in ordinary conditions. In a crisis, correlations, the tendency of prices to move together, rose sharply, extreme moves arrived together, and both lending and buyers disappeared at once.

Step 4: Incentives

Leverage made small edges look like large returns, which attracted capital and rewarded the partners. Lenders competed for the fund's business and gave it generous terms. Roman's point: when lenders compete for a famous borrower, the discipline that normally limits leverage weakens exactly when it is most needed.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The warning signs were structural rather than dramatic. The fund's size had grown so large that its own positions were a big share of some markets, making it hard to exit without moving prices against itself. Many of its trades depended on the same willingness of investors to take risk. Earlier crises in Asia in 1997 had shown how quickly markets could seize. And the fund's returns came from leverage on thin margins, which meant a modest adverse move on the whole book could consume its capital.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return came when losses forced the question of selling into a market that knew the fund had to sell. Once others could see its positions and its need, they had every reason to wait or to trade against it. Without fresh capital, the fund would have had to sell at whatever price the market offered. The time to reduce leverage was before Russia defaulted, while selling was still cheap.

Step 7: Root cause

The root cause was high leverage on concentrated exposure to one common risk, disguised as diversification. Each position was defensible; the sum, at that leverage, could not survive the one event that moved them all together.

Applying it to a developer

Worked example, hypothetical. A developer has 2,000,000 dollars of his own capital and borrows 2,000,000 dollars personally against his home and investments to fund equity in four condominium projects in one city, each with a construction loan of 70 percent of cost. A 20 percent fall in local condominium values does not cost him 20 percent. In each project, the lender's loan sits ahead of the equity, so a 20 percent fall in value may wipe out most of the equity. If the four projects together lose 3,000,000 dollars of equity, his own 2,000,000 is gone and he still owes 1,000,000 of the personal loan, secured on his home. Unlevered, the same downturn would have cost him a fraction of his wealth. The layers of borrowing turned a market decline into a personal insolvency.

Second worked example, hypothetical. The same developer with no personal borrowing and two projects instead of four, in two cities, loses equity in one project and is shaken but intact. The difference is not skill; it is leverage and concentration.

Roman's lens: the lenders were part of the concentration

Roman here. One more feature of the case matters for a developer. LTCM's lenders and trading counterparties were many of the same large institutions, and several of them held similar positions of their own. That is why a disorderly collapse worried them: forced selling by the fund would have hurt their own books, and its failure to pay would have hit them directly. Concentration ran both ways. For you, the parallel is a portfolio in which one lender funds every project. In a downturn, that lender reviews its whole exposure to you at once, and a problem on one loan colours its view of all of them. Spreading lenders, where the extra cost is reasonable, is part of spreading risk, and it gives you a second relationship when the first one tightens.

There is also a lesson about speed. The fund's losses came over weeks, not years. Developers think in project cycles of two or three years, but the moment when leverage bites can be very short: a lender's credit review, a sales freeze, a valuation. The time to reduce leverage is measured in calm months, not in crisis weeks.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is believing that many positions mean diversification, when they share the same underlying risk and the same lenders. The control is to stress the whole portfolio with one common shock and see whether you survive it, at your current leverage.

The beginner's mistake

Adding leverage because the previous deals worked. Past success under calm conditions is not evidence that your leverage can survive a crisis.

Callback

In Week 46, Ford and Roman studied leverage spirals and maturity walls in property, including General Growth Properties in 2009. LTCM is the same spiral in a different market: losses force sales, sales lower prices, lower prices create more losses, and only a reserve or fresh capital stops it.

Recap

LTCM, founded in 1994, lost most of its capital in 1998 after Russia's default sent its many similar trades against it at once; lenders recapitalised it in September 1998. The root cause was high leverage on concentrated exposure disguised as diversification. Rule 86.

Next: Roman, on The Money: how leverage and concentration change the range of outcomes, not just the average.
checklist: I stress my whole portfolio with one common shock, at current leverage.
I group positions by the condition they all depend on.
I count every layer of borrowing beneath my equity.
I never add leverage because recent deals went well.
I check whether my lenders are the same across positions.
I reduce leverage in calm conditions, while selling is still cheap.
I keep a reserve that lets me avoid selling into a forced market.
head: Field checklist
speak: Long-Term Capital Management was a hedge fund founded in 1994, with partners including Myron Scholes and Robert Merton, who shared the 1997 Nobel prize in economics. It made carefully modelled bets that small price gaps would narrow, and borrowed many times its capital to make thin margins into large returns. Its trades spanned many markets and looked diversified, but they all depended on calm markets. In August 1998 Russia defaulted and devalued, investors fled to safety, the gaps widened together, and the fund lost most of its capital. In September 1998 the Federal Reserve Bank of New York convened banks and brokers, who put in about 3.6 billion dollars for most of the fund. The root cause was high leverage on concentrated exposure disguised as diversification. For me, that means stressing my whole portfolio with one common shock at my real leverage, and never borrowing personally beneath equity that is already levered.
terms: Leverage — using borrowed money to increase the size of a position, which magnifies both gains and losses on your own capital.
Correlation — the tendency of two prices or assets to move together; in crises, many correlations rise sharply.
Forced seller — someone who must sell regardless of price, whom buyers can see and take advantage of.

hostile.q: You have four projects. Isn't that diversified?
hostile.a: Not if they share one city, one asset type and one lender. I stressed all four with a single local downturn and, at our current leverage, the equity losses would exceed my own capital and reach the personal loan. So I am not taking a fifth project in the same market, and I am repaying the personal loan before the next commitment.

rule: Rule 86: Never let the total of my personal borrowing and guarantees rest on positions that one common shock could hit together; before every new commitment, stress the whole portfolio with that single shock and stop if I would not survive it.

title: How Leverage and Concentration Change the Range of Outcomes, Not Just the Average
summary: Leverage and concentration can leave the expected return looking better while making the bad outcomes far worse. This lesson works through a hypothetical developer's portfolio under three structures and shows how the average, the severe case and the chance of ruin each move. The Wealth Ledger then turns the result into a personal balance sheet limit.
body:
An investor who looks only at the average return will choose more leverage and more concentration almost every time. An investor who looks at the severe case and the chance of ruin will often choose less. Survival lives in the tail, not the average.

Recall

Q. What does Rule 86 say?

A. Never let the total of personal borrowing and guarantees rest on positions one common shock could hit together; stress the whole portfolio with that shock before every new commitment and stop if you would not survive it.

Q. What is a forced-sale discount?

A. The gap between an asset's value to a patient seller and the price a buyer pays a seller who must sell quickly.

Q. What does a waiver of subrogation do?

A. It stops an insurer that pays a claim from suing the other parties named in the waiver to recover what it paid, which keeps project parties from suing each other through their insurers.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Roman. Lenders and good investors think in ranges because they have seen the bottom of the range. Developers often think in averages because the pro forma shows one number. This lesson shows, with hypothetical round numbers, why the same deals can make a developer wealthy or ruin him depending on how they are sized, spread and financed. All figures are illustrative and conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Three structures for the same capital

A developer has 3,000,000 dollars of his own capital. Each project, if it succeeds, returns 1.6 times the equity over its life; in a downturn, a project's equity is lost entirely. Assume, for teaching, that in any period there is a 20 percent chance of a local downturn that hits every project in one city at once.

Structure A, concentrated and levered. He borrows 2,000,000 dollars personally and puts 5,000,000 of equity into five projects in one city. Good outcome, 80 percent chance: 5,000,000 becomes 8,000,000; he repays 2,000,000 plus, say, 200,000 interest, and keeps 5,800,000. Bad outcome, 20 percent chance: all five projects lose their equity; he has nothing and still owes 2,200,000. Expected ending wealth: 0.8 times 5,800,000 is 4,640,000, plus 0.2 times minus 2,200,000, which is minus 440,000, for 4,200,000 dollars. Chance of ending below zero: 20 percent.

Structure B, concentrated, unlevered. He puts his 3,000,000 into three projects in one city. Good: 4,800,000. Bad: zero. Expected: 0.8 times 4,800,000, or 3,840,000 dollars. Chance of ending below zero: none, but a 20 percent chance of losing everything he invested.

Structure C, spread, unlevered, with a reserve. He keeps 600,000 in reserve and puts 2,400,000 into projects across two cities whose downturns, for teaching, are independent, 1,200,000 in each. Good in both, 64 percent chance: 2,400,000 becomes 3,840,000, plus the reserve, 4,440,000. Bad in one, 32 percent chance: 1,920,000 plus 600,000, which is 2,520,000. Bad in both, 4 percent chance: 600,000. Expected: about 2,842,000 plus 806,000 plus 24,000, roughly 3,672,000 dollars. Chance of ending below zero: none; worst case keeps 600,000.

Say that out loud now.

Reading the three columns

StructureExpected ending wealthWorst caseChance of ruin
A, levered, one cityabout 4,200,000owes 2,200,00020 percent
B, unlevered, one cityabout 3,840,000zero invested capital left20 percent of losing all invested
C, spread, with reserveabout 3,672,000600,000 leftnone

Structure A has the highest average and the worst tail. On average it wins; one time in five it ends the career and follows him home. Structure C gives up about 528,000 dollars of expected wealth against A and buys the certainty that he is still in business after the worst case. The question is not which column is best in general. It is which column you can live through, and only you can answer that.

Why the average misleads over a career

A career is not one period. It is many. A strategy with a 20 percent chance of ruin each period has, over five independent periods, about a 67 percent chance of ruin at least once: 1 minus 0.8 to the power of 5, which is 1 minus about 0.33. The high average of Structure A is earned only by those who survive, and most will not. This is why Rule 86 asks whether you survive the common shock, not whether the expected return is attractive. Repeated exposure to a small chance of ruin is not small.

The assumption that does most of the work

Structure C beat the others in the tail because the two cities' downturns were assumed independent. That is the assumption to challenge hardest. Two cities in one country may share interest rates, lenders, buyers and policy, so their downturns may arrive together, and in a national or global shock they often do. Rerun Structure C with the two markets perfectly correlated: both good 80 percent of the time, both bad 20 percent. Good: 3,840,000 plus 600,000, or 4,440,000. Bad: 600,000. Expected: 0.8 times 4,440,000 is 3,552,000, plus 120,000, for 3,672,000 dollars, the same average as before. What changes is the tail. With independent markets, the 600,000 outcome had a 4 percent chance; with correlated markets it has a 20 percent chance. The reserve still prevents ruin, which is why it matters more than the second city. Diversification helps only as much as the risks genuinely differ; the reserve helps whether they differ or not.

Leverage changes the shape, not just the size

Leverage magnifies gains and losses, but it also adds a new outcome: owing money after the asset is gone. Unlevered, the worst case is losing what you invested. Levered personally, the worst case is losing what you invested and then losing what you had kept outside the deal, including, through security and guarantees, your home. That new outcome is what changes a bad year into a ruined decade.

What a lender reads from the same table

A lender asked to fund Structure A sees the same arithmetic from the other side. Its borrower's equity is partly borrowed, its guarantor's assets are pledged elsewhere, and its project shares a market with four others the guarantor is also exposed to. The guarantee it is relying on is weakest in exactly the scenario in which it would be called. Experienced credit officers price that, through higher equity requirements, tighter covenants or a refusal. A developer running Structure C, with a visible reserve and spread exposure, offers a guarantee that is still worth something in a downturn, and is often rewarded with better terms.

Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, add a line showing your net worth after the common shock: every position in the same market losing its equity at once, every guarantee in that market called, and every personal loan still owing. If that figure is below zero, or below the liquidity floor you set in Week 7, you are running Structure A whether you meant to or not. The adjustment is not to stop developing; it is to change the sizing, the spread or the borrowing until the after-shock figure is one you can live with.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is choosing the structure with the best average without looking at the chance of ruin and how it compounds over a career. The control is a three-column table, expected, worst case and chance of ruin, for every allocation decision.

The beginner's mistake

Treating separate projects as independent because they have separate companies and separate loans. Legal separation does not make their risks independent if one local downturn can hit them all.

Callback

In Week 44, Roman taught base, downside and severe cases for a single project. Today applies the same thinking to the whole portfolio, and adds one thing the single-project stress test cannot show: how the chance of ruin compounds over a career of repeated bets.

Recap

Leverage and concentration raise the average while worsening the tail. Compare structures by expected wealth, worst case and chance of ruin, remember that repeated small chances of ruin compound, and keep an after-shock line on your balance sheet.

Next: LEX, on The Rules: personal guarantees, joint and several liability and the cross-default clauses that link your deals together.
checklist: I compare allocation choices by expected wealth, worst case and chance of ruin.
I calculate how a chance of ruin compounds over several periods.
My balance sheet shows my net worth after the common shock.
I check the after-shock figure against my liquidity floor.
I treat separate companies as one risk if one downturn can hit them all.
I count owing money after the asset is gone as a distinct outcome of personal leverage.
I confirm my allocation with a licensed adviser before acting.
head: Field checklist
speak: With hypothetical numbers, a developer with 3,000,000 dollars can borrow personally and concentrate in one city, invest unlevered in one city, or spread across two cities with a reserve. The levered, concentrated structure has the highest average, about 4,200,000 dollars, but a 20 percent chance of ending in debt. The spread structure with a reserve averages about 3,672,000 and never leaves him with less than 600,000. Over a career the difference grows, because a 20 percent chance of ruin each period becomes about a two-in-three chance over five periods. Personal leverage also adds a new outcome: owing money after the asset is gone. So I compare every allocation by three numbers, expected wealth, worst case and chance of ruin. And on my balance sheet I keep a line showing my net worth after the common shock, checked against my liquidity floor, with a licensed adviser before I act.
terms: Tail — the extreme, low-probability outcomes at the edges of a range, where ruin usually lives.
Chance of ruin — the probability that a strategy ends with nothing left, or with debts larger than assets.
Expected value — the probability-weighted average of all outcomes, which can hide a severe tail.

hostile.q: Structure A has the highest expected return. Why wouldn't you take it?
hostile.a: Because the average is earned only by those who survive. On these numbers, A carries a 20 percent chance of ending in debt each period, which compounds to about two in three over five periods. I'd rather give up about half a million dollars of expected wealth and still be developing in ten years.

title: The Paper That Links Your Deals: Guarantees, Joint and Several Liability and Cross-Default
summary: Concentration is not only economic. Contracts can link separate deals legally, so that a failure in one reaches the others and reaches you. This lesson teaches personal guarantees, joint and several liability, cross-default and cross-collateralisation as concepts, and how to read for them before you sign.
body:
You can spread your deals across cities and still have them tied together by a few sentences in the loan documents. Read for those sentences, because they decide whether one bad project stays one bad project.

Recall

Q. Why can a strategy with a 20 percent chance of ruin each period be so dangerous over a career?

A. Because the chance compounds: over five independent periods it becomes about a two-in-three chance of ruin at least once.

Q. What is a condition precedent in a notice clause?

A. A requirement that notice be given in the specified way and time before a right, such as an extension of time, exists. Whether it is enforced as written depends on the governing law.

Q. What does an unforeseen ground conditions clause typically do?

A. It gives the contractor relief, in time and sometimes money, for physical conditions a competent contractor could not reasonably have foreseen from the information provided. The test is in the wording.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is LEX. Roman showed this week that concentration lives in common risks. The law adds another kind: contractual linkage. Separate companies, separate loans and separate projects can be joined by guarantees and default clauses so that one failure triggers the others. Everything below is conceptual. The effect of any clause depends on its exact wording and the governing law, so verify each point against the primary source, and against your own documents, before you rely on it.

The personal guarantee, revisited from the portfolio side

In plain English: a guarantee is your promise to pay if the borrower does not, and every guarantee you sign draws on the same pocket.

A personal guarantee makes you liable for a borrower's obligation if it fails to meet it. Guarantees vary: they may cover the whole loan, a capped amount, completion, cost overruns or specific bad acts, and they may burn off at a milestone. From the portfolio side, the key point is that every guarantee you sign, on every project, is a claim on the same personal assets. Three capped guarantees of 500,000 dollars each, on three separate projects, are 1,500,000 dollars of potential calls on one balance sheet. Lenders on each project may not know about the others unless you disclose them, and they will often ask.

Joint and several liability

In plain English: if you sign with others, the lender may be able to collect the whole amount from you alone.

Where two or more guarantors are jointly and severally liable, the creditor can usually pursue any one of them for the full amount, leaving that guarantor to seek contribution from the others. Worked example, hypothetical. You and two partners jointly and severally guarantee a 1,500,000-dollar shortfall. You each think of your share as 500,000 dollars. If one partner is insolvent and the other has moved assets beyond reach, the lender may collect the full 1,500,000 from you, and your claim against the others is worth only what they can pay. Your real exposure is the full amount, not your share. Ask for several liability, limited to your share, where you can, and price the difference if the lender will not agree.

Say that out loud now.

Cross-default and cross-collateralisation

In plain English: some loans say that a default anywhere is a default here, or that one property secures another's loan.

A cross-default clause makes a default under one agreement an event of default under another, so a problem on project one can let project two's lender demand repayment even though project two is performing. Cross-default can be drafted narrowly, covering only the same borrower's other loans with the same lender above a threshold, or broadly, covering any debt of any group company or guarantor. Cross-collateralisation goes further: security over one property stands behind another's loan, so a failure on one can lead to enforcement against both.

Second worked example, hypothetical. You guarantee a loan on project one and a different lender's loan on project two. Project two's loan contains a broad cross-default covering any default by the guarantor on any obligation over a modest threshold. Project one overruns, its lender calls your guarantee, and you cannot pay within the time allowed. That is now a default under project two's loan as well, even though project two is on time and on budget. One problem has become two, through the guarantor. The concentration was created by a definition in a loan agreement, not by the market.

Reading for linkage before you sign

Build one table for your portfolio. For every loan, list the borrower, the lender, every guarantor and the guarantee type and cap, whether liability is joint and several, the cross-default scope and threshold, any cross-collateral, and the events that trigger personal recourse. Then trace a failure: if project one defaults tomorrow, which other agreements are triggered, and which of your personal assets are exposed? The table often reveals that a portfolio which looks spread out is legally one position.

Negotiating points, all commercial practice rather than standards: cap each guarantee and add a burn-off; seek several rather than joint and several liability; limit cross-default to the same borrower and the same lender, above a meaningful threshold, with a cure period; exclude guarantor defaults from project-level cross-default; and avoid cross-collateralisation unless it buys something you need.

A worked trace through the table

Hypothetical, three projects. Project one: lender X, borrower company one, guarantee by you capped at 400,000, several, cross-default limited to company one's loans with lender X. Project two: lender Y, borrower company two, guarantee by you and a partner, joint and several, capped at 600,000, cross-default covering any default by any guarantor on any debt above 100,000. Project three: lender X again, borrower company three, cross-collateralised with project one.

Now trace a failure on project one. Lender X calls your 400,000 guarantee. Because project three is cross-collateralised with project one, lender X may also look to project three's property. If you take more than the allowed time to pay the 400,000, that is a guarantor default above 100,000, which triggers the cross-default in project two, so lender Y can accelerate a performing loan, and because that guarantee is joint and several, it may pursue you for the full 600,000. One problem has reached all three projects and up to 1,000,000 dollars of your personal assets. Before the trace, the portfolio looked like three separate risks of 400,000, 300,000 and nothing. After it, it is one linked exposure.

Disclosure duties

Loan agreements commonly require you to disclose other guarantees and indebtedness and to keep that disclosure true. A false or stale representation about your other obligations can itself be an event of default and, in serious cases, raise questions of misrepresentation. Keep your guarantee register current and give each lender the same accurate picture.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer, as borrower's and guarantor's counsel, on every guarantee and cross-default clause.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a broad cross-default clause that turns one project's problem into a default across your portfolio through you as guarantor. The control is the linkage table, reviewed before each new loan, and negotiating narrow cross-default scope.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking of a joint and several guarantee as your share of the total. Assume the creditor can collect the whole amount from you, and size your reserve and your limits on that basis.

Callback

In Week 39, Priya taught events of default and covenants in a construction loan. Today places those clauses across a portfolio: an event of default is not confined to one loan if a cross-default clause carries it to the next, and the guarantor is usually the bridge.

Recap

Guarantees draw on one pocket; joint and several liability can make your exposure the whole amount; cross-default and cross-collateral link deals legally. Build the linkage table and negotiate narrow terms before signing.

Next: Roman, on The Numbers: reverse engineering a position size from the loss you can bear.
checklist: I keep a register of every guarantee I have signed, with type, cap and burn-off.
I assume joint and several liability means I could pay the whole amount.
I know the cross-default scope and threshold in every loan.
I know whether any property secures another project's loan.
I trace a single project default through my whole linkage table.
I negotiate narrow cross-default and several liability where I can.
I give every lender the same accurate picture of my other guarantees.
head: Field checklist
speak: Spreading deals across cities does not help if the loan documents tie them together. Every personal guarantee draws on the same pocket, so three capped guarantees of 500,000 each are 1,500,000 of potential calls on me. If I sign jointly and severally with partners, the lender can usually collect the whole amount from me and leave me to chase them, so my real exposure is the total, not my share. A cross-default clause can make a default on one loan a default on another, and if it covers guarantor defaults, a called guarantee on project one can put a healthy project two in default. Cross-collateral lets one property stand behind another's loan. So I keep one linkage table for the portfolio, trace a single default through it before every new loan, and negotiate caps, burn-offs, several liability and narrow cross-default, with a lawyer.
terms: Joint and several liability — liability under which a creditor can recover the whole amount from any one of the obligors.
Cross-default — a clause making a default under one agreement an event of default under another.
Cross-collateralisation — using security over one asset to secure the debt of another loan or project.

hostile.q: Your other project is performing. Why are you worried about its loan?
hostile.a: Because its cross-default clause covers any default by me as guarantor above a low threshold. If my guarantee on the overrunning project is called and I can't pay in time, the healthy project defaults too. I'm funding the guarantee from reserve so it never becomes a default, and I'm asking the lender to narrow the clause to this borrower and this lender, with a cure period.

title: Reverse Engineering a Position Size from the Loss You Can Bear
summary: Start from the finished outcome you are willing to live with after a severe shock, and work backward to the largest position, guarantee and personal borrowing you can take. A step-by-step calculation with hypothetical round numbers, ending in a one-line allocation limit.
body:
Most people size a deal from the opportunity forward. The safer method runs backward: decide what you must still have after the worst realistic year, and let that number tell you how large the deal can be.

Recall

Q. What is cross-default?

A. A clause making a default under one agreement an event of default under another, which can carry a problem on one project to another through the borrower or guarantor.

Q. What does adjusted net worth mean?

A. Net worth reduced by the forced-sale discount you would suffer if contingent calls arrived without enough reserve.

Q. What is force majeure?

A. A contract clause that relieves a party from liability for delay or non-performance caused by defined events beyond its control, with effect depending on the wording and governing law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Roman. This is an even week, so we reverse engineer: start from a finished outcome and work backward. The outcome here is not a building. It is your balance sheet the year after a severe shock. If you fix that first, every later decision about a deal becomes arithmetic rather than temptation. All figures are hypothetical round numbers, and a licensed adviser is required before you act.

Step 1: State the finished outcome

A hypothetical developer has a net worth of 6,000,000 dollars: 1,000,000 in tiers 1 and 2, 500,000 in his home equity, and 4,500,000 in project equity. He writes down the outcome he must still have after a severe local downturn: tiers 1 and 2 intact at 1,000,000, his home untouched, and no personal debt outstanding. Everything else, he accepts, can be lost. This is his floor. It is his choice, and it would be different for another person.

Step 2: Define the severe shock

With his advisers, he defines the severe case for his market: in a deep local downturn, a project in construction loses all its equity, and its cost-overrun guarantee is called at the cap. A completed, stabilised project loses 30 percent of its equity value but is not forced to sell. These assumptions are illustrative; a real severe case is built from the market and the project.

Step 3: Work back to what can be at risk

Since tiers 1 and 2 and the home must survive, the most that can be lost in the shock is the 4,500,000 of project equity plus nothing else. But guarantees are paid from somewhere. If a guarantee is called, the money comes from tiers 1 and 2, which breaks the floor. So the floor implies a rule: total guarantee calls in the severe case must be met by something other than the protected reserve, or must be zero. He chooses to fund them from a separate guarantee reserve. If he has none beyond the protected 1,000,000, his guarantee capacity is zero. He adds a dedicated guarantee reserve of 600,000 dollars, moved from project equity as it is realised. That sets his total severe-case guarantee capacity at 600,000.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Work back to the position size

Now a new project arrives, asking for equity and a cost-overrun guarantee capped at 400,000 dollars. He already has one project in construction with a guarantee capped at 300,000. Severe case: both called, 700,000, against a guarantee reserve of 600,000. He is 100,000 over. He can ask for the new cap to be 300,000 dollars, bringing the total to exactly 600,000, or wait until the first guarantee burns off. Working backward from the floor gave him a specific negotiating target: 300,000, not "as low as possible".

Step 5: Work back to the concentration limit

Next, concentration. If both projects in construction are in the same city, one shock hits both. If they were in different, independent markets, a severe case might hit one at a time. He is not yet able to diversify across markets, so he treats them as one exposure and keeps the guarantee total inside 600,000. He also checks his equity exposure: if both construction projects lose all their equity, how much is that? Suppose 1,200,000 and 1,000,000, so 2,200,000. His stabilised project held 2,300,000 of equity, but the 600,000 guarantee reserve was realised from it, so it now holds 1,700,000; 30 percent of that is 510,000. Total severe loss: 2,710,000 dollars of equity plus up to 600,000 of guarantee calls from the dedicated reserve.

Step 6: Check the finished outcome

After the shock: tiers 1 and 2, 1,000,000, intact. Home, 500,000, intact. Guarantee reserve spent: 600,000 gone. Project equity: 4,500,000 minus 600,000 moved to the reserve leaves 3,900,000, minus 2,710,000 lost, leaving 1,190,000. Personal debt: none. Net worth after the shock: 1,000,000 plus 500,000 plus 1,190,000, which is 2,690,000 dollars. It is a severe loss, more than half of his wealth, but the floor holds: reserves and home intact, no personal debt. He can rebuild.

Step 7: What breaks the floor

Now test the mistake. Suppose instead he borrowed 1,000,000 dollars personally to fund the new project's equity. In the severe case that equity is lost and the loan remains. He must repay it from somewhere, and the only unprotected assets left are the 1,190,000 of surviving project equity, which he may be forced to sell at a discount. If the discount is 25 percent, selling all of it raises only about 893,000, so he still owes about 107,000, which reaches his reserve or his home, and he has sold every remaining project to get there. The floor breaks. The reverse engineering shows that personal borrowing to fund equity is not allowed under his own floor, however good the deal looks.

Step 7a: Why the floor must be written before the deal

Notice what the calculation did. It did not ask whether the new project was a good deal; it may be excellent. It asked whether the developer could survive the project going badly alongside everything else he owns. That question is easy to answer honestly in a quiet week and very hard to answer honestly when a partner is waiting and the vendor's deadline is close. People who set the floor after seeing the deal tend to set it just low enough to allow the deal. That is why the floor, the shock and the guarantee capacity are fixed in advance, in writing, and changed only through a deliberate review. The arithmetic is simple; the discipline is in its timing.

A practical routine: run this calculation every quarter and every time a guarantee is signed, released or burns off, and keep the latest version on one page beside your wealth architecture. When a new deal arrives, you do not start from a blank sheet; you start from a capacity figure that already exists, and the only question is whether the deal fits inside it.

Step 8: The one-line limit

He writes the result as his allocation policy: "Severe-case guarantee calls in total may not exceed my dedicated guarantee reserve, currently 600,000 dollars; no personal borrowing to fund equity; projects in one market are treated as one exposure." Every future deal is checked against those three sentences.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is defining the floor and then funding guarantees from it. The control is a separate guarantee reserve, sized to the total severe-case calls, so the protected reserve is never the source of a call.

The beginner's mistake

Running the calculation once and not re-running it when a new guarantee is signed or an old one burns off. The limit moves with every change.

Callback

In Week 17, Sage taught reverse engineering a deal from public information, starting from the price and working back to the implied land value. Today uses the same technique on yourself: start from the balance sheet you must keep, and work back to the deal you can take.

Recap

Fix the outcome you must keep after a severe shock, define the shock, work back to guarantee capacity, position size and concentration, check the finished outcome, and test what breaks it. Write the result in three sentences.

Next: Warrick, on The Room: the partner who wants you all in on one deal, with a personal guarantee.
checklist: I have written the balance sheet I must keep after a severe shock.
I fund guarantee calls from a dedicated reserve, never from the protected floor.
I know my total severe-case guarantee capacity in dollars.
I treat projects in one market as one exposure until I am genuinely diversified.
I test every new deal against my floor before negotiating its terms.
I use the floor to set a specific negotiating target for each guarantee cap.
I re-run the calculation whenever a guarantee is signed or burns off.
head: Field checklist
speak: I size deals backward. First I write the outcome I must keep after a severe local downturn: in this hypothetical, 1,000,000 dollars of reserves intact, my home untouched and no personal debt. Then I define the shock: projects in construction lose all their equity and their guarantees are called at the cap, while stabilised projects lose 30 percent. Because guarantee calls must not come from the protected reserve, I hold a separate guarantee reserve, here 600,000, and that becomes my total guarantee capacity. A new project asking for a 400,000 cap on top of an existing 300,000 is 100,000 over, so I negotiate the cap to 300,000 or wait for the first to burn off. I check the result: after the shock I would keep about 2,690,000 and my floor holds. Then I test personal borrowing to fund equity, and it breaks the floor, so I rule it out.
terms: Floor — the minimum balance sheet you commit to keeping after a severe shock, set in advance.
Guarantee capacity — the total severe-case guarantee calls you can meet from a dedicated reserve without touching your floor.
Allocation policy — a short written statement of the limits every new investment must satisfy.

hostile.q: Why does it matter whether the guarantee cap is 300,000 or 400,000? You'll never be called.
hostile.a: Because my policy says the total severe-case calls must fit inside a dedicated guarantee reserve of 600,000 dollars, and with my existing guarantee, 400,000 takes me to 700,000. If I were called on both, the extra 100,000 would come from the reserve that protects my family. At 300,000 the deal fits; at 400,000 I'd wait until my first guarantee burns off.

title: The Partner Who Wants You All In: Saying No Without Losing the Deal
summary: A realistic scene: a respected partner brings a strong deal and asks you to put most of your liquid wealth into it and sign a joint and several personal guarantee. How to hold your allocation limits, what to offer instead, what never to say, and how to keep the relationship.
body:
The hardest allocation decisions are not made at a spreadsheet. They are made across a table from someone you respect, about a deal you like, with a deadline. Your limits must be strong enough to survive that room.

Recall

Q. In the reverse engineer, why is a separate guarantee reserve needed?

A. So that guarantee calls are never paid from the protected reserve that the floor says must survive a severe shock.

Q. What should you say before any product is presented in a banker's annual review?

A. That the agenda is your plan first and that you will not decide anything in the meeting.

Q. What does a limitation of liability clause do, and what does it leave?

A. It caps what one party can recover from another, often at the contract sum or insurance limits, leaving any loss above the cap with the party who suffers it, subject to exceptions under the wording and the law.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Warrick. Every rule from this week will be tested by a person, not a market. A partner with a strong record, a good deal and a real deadline is the most dangerous person to your allocation policy, precisely because the request is reasonable. This scene shows how to say no to the size while saying yes to the relationship. Everything here is conceptual; a licensed adviser and a lawyer are required before you act.

The setup

This is a composite scene with hypothetical facts. Your partner, Marcus, has delivered three projects well. He has a site under conditional contract for a 30,000,000-dollar residential building. He wants you to put in 2,000,000 dollars of equity, which is most of your tiers 1 and 2, and to sign a joint and several completion and cost-overrun guarantee with him for the senior loan. The vendor's condition deadline is in ten days. Your allocation policy says no single deal may cost you more than 15 percent of net worth in a severe case, no protected reserve may fund equity, and guarantee calls must fit inside your dedicated guarantee reserve.

Opening

Start with the relationship and the deal, then the limit: "Marcus, this is a good site and you have earned my trust. I want to be in it. I can't be in it at the size you've proposed, and I want to show you why and what I can do instead."

That order matters. Agreement on the deal comes first, so the limit is heard as a fact about you, not a judgment about him.

The lines to say

On size: "My rule is that no single deal can cost me more than 15 percent of my net worth in a severe case. At 2,000,000 of equity plus a joint and several guarantee, a bad outcome would cost me far more than that, and it would come out of the reserve that protects my family. I can commit 800,000 dollars of equity."

On the guarantee: "I can sign a several guarantee for my share, capped at a figure that fits my guarantee reserve, with a burn-off at completion. I can't sign joint and several for the whole loan, because if anything happened to you, the lender could come to me for all of it."

On the gap: "That leaves 1,200,000 of equity to find. I would like to help you find it, and I have two people I can introduce who invest at that size."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say, "I don't trust the deal," if what you mean is that the size is wrong. It insults the partner and is not the reason. Never say, "Let me see if I can stretch," which tells him your limit is negotiable and invites pressure. Never say, "I'll guarantee it if I have to," which concedes the guarantee before you have tried to shape it. And never apologise for having a limit; explain it, once, and hold it.

The question behind the question

When Marcus says, "Are you committed to this partnership?", the question behind it is whether your limit is about him. Answer: "Completely, which is why I want to be in this deal and the next ten. Staying inside my limits is how I make sure I am still here for them." When he says, "The vendor won't wait," the question behind it is whether urgency will move you. Answer: "Then let's use the ten days to find the other 1,200,000, not to change my number." When he says, "The lender insists on joint and several," the question behind it is whether you will test that. Answer: "Let's ask. If it's truly non-negotiable, we size the guarantee and my equity together so that the whole of my exposure still fits."

When to stay silent

After you name your number, 800,000, stop. Let him respond. The silence tells him the number is considered, not opening. If he pushes, restate the reason in one sentence and stop again. Do not fill the pause with qualifications that sound like a counter-offer to yourself.

Holding your state

A friend's disappointment pulls harder than a stranger's pressure. Notice the pull. Keep your allocation policy in front of you, written, and refer to it: "This is the page I wrote before I saw any deal." Pointing to a rule you made in calm conditions takes the decision out of the room and makes it less personal for both of you. Speak slowly and keep your shoulders down.

If he walks away

Sometimes the partner will not accept the smaller yes and takes the deal elsewhere. That is an acceptable outcome, and you should be able to say so to yourself in advance. A deal you were not in cannot ruin you. Thank him, wish the project well, and keep the door open: "I hope it does brilliantly. I'm ready for the next one at a size that fits." Partners who see you hold a limit calmly often trust you more afterwards, because they know your commitments are real.

After the meeting

Write a short note the same day confirming what you offered: equity of 800,000 dollars, a several guarantee for your share with a cap and a burn-off, and introductions to two investors. Then record the decision in your decision journal.

Decision journals

This month's thread is the decision journal. Write the entry before you know the outcome: the deal, the size you chose, the reason, the alternatives you rejected, what you expect to happen, and how you felt in the room. Date it.

Review the entry when the project completes. If you were right to be cautious, the journal shows your reasons held up. If the deal did better than you expected, the journal shows whether your reasons were wrong or only your luck was. Either way, you learn from the reasoning rather than from the result, which is the only way a single outcome teaches anything.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is abandoning a written limit because the person asking is trusted and the deal is good. The control is to make the limit public in the room, point to it as a rule made in advance, and offer a constructive alternative.

The beginner's mistake

Saying a flat no, which loses the deal and strains the partnership, or a flat yes, which breaks the policy. The professional answer is a smaller yes with help to close the gap.

Callback

In Week 66, Kema and JAX taught interests versus positions and the BATNA. Marcus's position is 2,000,000 dollars from you; his interest is closing the equity in ten days. Your answer serves his interest without accepting his position, and your BATNA, staying out, is acceptable to you, which is why you can hold the line calmly.

Recap

Agree on the deal first, then state your limit as a rule made in advance. Offer a smaller equity commitment, a several and capped guarantee, and help to fill the gap. Stay silent after your number, and write the decision in your journal before you know the outcome.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on capital allocation, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I agree on the deal before I state the limit.
I state my limit as a rule I wrote before seeing the deal.
I offer a specific smaller commitment rather than a flat no.
I seek several, capped guarantees with a burn-off.
I stay silent after naming my number.
I offer help to close the gap, such as introductions.
I write a decision journal entry before I know the outcome.
head: Field checklist
speak: A respected partner brings a strong deal and asks me for 2,000,000 dollars of equity, most of my reserves, plus a joint and several guarantee, with a ten-day deadline. I start with the relationship and the deal: it is a good site, and I want to be in it. Then I state my limit as a rule I wrote before I saw any deal: no single deal can cost me more than 15 percent of my net worth in a severe case, and my protected reserve never funds equity. I offer 800,000 of equity, a several guarantee for my share with a cap and a burn-off, and introductions to two investors who could fill the gap. I never say I don't trust the deal, never offer to stretch, and never concede the guarantee early. After naming my number, I stop talking. Then I write the decision and my reasons in my journal before I know how the deal turns out.
terms: Several liability — liability limited to each obligor's own share, as opposed to joint and several liability for the whole.
Decision journal — a dated record of a decision, its reasons, the alternatives and the expected outcome, reviewed later.
Smaller yes — a constructive counter-offer that keeps the relationship and the deal while staying inside your limits.

hostile.q: If you really believed in this deal, wouldn't you put more in?
hostile.a: I do believe in it, which is why I'm committing 800,000 dollars and helping you find the rest. My limit isn't about this deal; it's a rule I wrote before I saw it, so that no single project can cost my family more than it can bear. That rule is what lets me keep investing with you for the next ten deals.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 86 Review: Position Size, Concentration and Personal Leverage
summary: Six questions on capital allocation, a recap of each lesson, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical allocation memo with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom drill explaining why a developer limits his position sizes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: decide what you must keep after the worst realistic year, and let that number set how much of you goes into any deal, any market and any borrowing.

Recall

Q. In the partner scene, what should you offer instead of a flat no?

A. A smaller yes: a specific equity commitment inside your limit, a several and capped guarantee with a burn-off, and help to fill the gap.

Q. What does Rule 85 say about reserves?

A. Never keep the emergency reserve only in a currency or banking system that the shock you fear could devalue or freeze.

Q. What is the difference between an indemnity and a limitation of liability?

A. An indemnity is a promise to cover another party's specified losses; a limitation of liability caps what one party can recover. One shifts loss toward a party, the other limits how much loss can be shifted.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is Kema. This week is where your wealth architecture meets your deal flow. Every future opportunity will test the limits you set here. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What are the three decisions of capital allocation?

Answer: Position size, meaning how much of your wealth is in one deal including realistic guarantee calls; concentration, meaning how much is exposed to one common risk; and personal leverage, meaning debt you owe or guarantee personally.

Question 2. How do you set a position size?

Answer: From loss, not opportunity. Decide the most a severe case may cost you, as a share of net worth or against your floor, then size equity and guarantees so the severe case stays inside it.

Question 3. What was the root cause of LTCM's failure in 1998?

Answer: High leverage on concentrated exposure to one common risk, calm markets, disguised as diversification across many trades. Russia's default in August 1998 moved them all against the fund at once. Rule 86.

Question 4. Why is the average return a dangerous guide?

Answer: Because leverage and concentration can raise the average while worsening the tail, and a chance of ruin compounds over repeated periods. Compare expected wealth, worst case and chance of ruin together.

Question 5. How can contracts concentrate your risk?

Answer: Through personal guarantees that all draw on one balance sheet, joint and several liability that can make you pay the whole, cross-default that carries one default to other loans, and cross-collateral that lets one property secure another's loan.

Question 6. Why should guarantee calls be paid from a dedicated reserve?

Answer: So that the protected reserve, which your floor says must survive a severe shock, is never the source of a call. The dedicated reserve then sets your total guarantee capacity.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Warrick, with Roman, framed capital allocation as position size, concentration and personal leverage. Ford and Roman took Long-Term Capital Management in 1998, giving Rule 86. Roman showed how leverage and concentration change the range of outcomes and how ruin compounds. LEX taught guarantees, joint and several liability and cross-default. Roman reverse engineered a position size from a floor. Warrick ran the partner who wanted you all in, and introduced the decision journal.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical allocation memo and find the defects before reading on.

Allocation memo. Net worth 6,000,000 dollars. We are well diversified across five projects, all mid-rise condominiums in the same city, funded by our usual lender. New project: we will take 1,500,000 dollars of equity, funded by a 1,000,000-dollar personal loan against my home and 500,000 from our emergency reserve. Guarantee: joint and several with my two partners for the full loan; my share is one third. The loan's cross-default clause covers any guarantor default; acceptable, as the other projects are performing. Expected return is 1.8 times equity; downside not modelled because the market is strong.

The defects. First, five projects in one city, one asset type and one lender are concentrated, not diversified; one local downturn hits all five. Second, the personal loan against the home funds equity in a levered project, adding a layer of personal leverage that can leave debt after the equity is gone. Third, the emergency reserve funds equity, breaking the floor. Fourth, joint and several liability means the exposure is the whole loan, not one third. Fifth, a cross-default clause covering any guarantor default links the healthy projects to this one through the guarantor; their current performance does not protect them. Sixth, the downside is not modelled, and a strong market is the condition in which it is most often ignored. Seventh, the memo states only an expected return, with no worst case and no chance of ruin. Eighth, nothing checks the total guarantee exposure against a dedicated guarantee reserve.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a new investor who asks, "Why do you keep your positions so small relative to your net worth?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because in development the deals are large, the outcomes are lumpy, and I usually guarantee part of the debt. So I decide in advance what I must keep after a severe local downturn, my reserves, my home and no personal debt, and I work backward from that. No single deal may cost me more than a fixed share of my net worth in a severe case. I group projects by what would make them fail together, city, asset type and lender, and treat each group as one exposure. I don't borrow personally to fund equity, because that turns a market decline into debt after the asset is gone. And I read the loan documents for cross-default and joint and several guarantees, because contracts can tie separate deals together. The average return of a more aggressive approach is higher, but its chance of ruin compounds over a career. I would rather still be developing in ten years."

Notice what the model answer does not do. It does not claim the strategy maximises returns, and it does not criticise more aggressive developers. It states the trade plainly: a lower average in exchange for survival. Investors who have lived through a downturn tend to find that reassuring rather than timid, because they have met the developers who chose the other column.

Score your own answer. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name all three decisions? Did you explain why the average misleads? Did you mention contractual linkage? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is letting a good deal or a trusted partner rewrite limits you set in calm conditions. The control is the written allocation policy, a cooling-off period to change it, and a decision journal entry for every exception.

Connecting the two weeks

Last week sized the reserves; this week sized the bets. The two meet in one number: the dedicated guarantee reserve. It belongs to wealth architecture as part of tier 2, and it belongs to capital allocation as the capacity that limits every new guarantee. If you can say that number from memory, and say which deals currently draw on it, you understand both weeks.

The beginner's mistake

Calling a set of similar projects diversified. Count common risks, not project names.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick asked you to define your own liquidity floor and what enough means. This week turned the floor into a limit on every deal: the floor is no longer a feeling about safety; it is the number that sizes your next position.

Recap

Size positions from the loss you can bear, group exposures by common risk, avoid personal borrowing beneath levered equity, read for contractual linkage, and compare choices by worst case and chance of ruin as well as the average. Rule 86 keeps one shock from reaching everything you own.

head: The six questions
speak: Capital allocation is three decisions: how much of me goes into one deal, how much of my wealth is exposed to one common risk, and how much personal borrowing sits behind it. I set position size from loss: I decide what I must keep after a severe local downturn, my reserves, my home and no personal debt, and size each deal's equity and guarantees so the severe case stays inside that. I group projects by what would make them fail together and treat each group as one exposure. I do not borrow personally to fund equity in projects that are already levered, because that leaves debt after the asset is gone, which is the lesson of LTCM in 1998. I read loan documents for joint and several guarantees and cross-default, because contracts can tie separate deals together. And I compare every choice by expected wealth, worst case and chance of ruin, because a chance of ruin compounds over a career.
terms: Capital allocation — deciding how much of your wealth goes into each investment, each kind of risk and each layer of borrowing.
Common shock — a single event, such as a local downturn, that hits several positions at once.
Cooling-off period — a deliberate delay required before changing a written limit, so the change is not made under pressure.

hostile.q: Your memo calls five condominium projects in one city diversified. Is it?
hostile.a: No. They share one city, one asset type and one lender, so one local downturn hits all five at once; that is one exposure. I've rewritten the memo to treat them as a single group, model the severe case for the whole group, and check the total guarantees against my dedicated reserve before taking anything new in that market.
